paragraphs: Very early, at nine o’clock in the morning, five days after the trial, Alyosha went to Katerina Ivanovna’s. He had a matter of great importance to both of them to talk over, and a message to give her. She sat and talked with him in the very room where she had once received Grushenka. In the next room Ivan Fyodorovitch lay unconscious, in a high fever. Right after the scene at the trial, Katerina Ivanovna had ordered the sick, unconscious man carried to her house. She ignored the gossip and general disapproval of the public, which she knew were bound to follow. Of the two relatives who lived with her, one had left for Moscow right after the scene in court, and the other had stayed. But even if both had gone, Katerina Ivanovna would have held to her decision and gone on nursing the sick man, sitting by him day and night. Varvinsky and Herzenstube were treating him. The famous doctor had gone back to Moscow, refusing to give an opinion on how the illness would end. The doctors encouraged Katerina Ivanovna and Alyosha, but it was plain they could not yet give them any firm hope of recovery.

Alyosha came to see his sick brother twice a day. But this time he had particularly urgent business. He could see how hard it would be to raise the subject, yet he was in a great hurry. He had another appointment that morning which could not be put off, so there was no time to lose.

They had been talking for a quarter of an hour. Katerina Ivanovna was pale and terribly tired, and at the same time in a state of hysterical excitement. She had a feeling already about why Alyosha had come to her.

“Don’t worry about his decision,” she said to Alyosha, with confident emphasis. “One way or another he is bound to come to it. He must escape. That unhappy man, that hero of honor and principle—not he, not Dmitri Fyodorovitch, but the man lying on the other side of that door, who has sacrificed himself for his brother,” Katya added, with flashing eyes, “told me the whole plan of escape long ago. You know he has already started negotiations.... I’ve told you something about it already.... You see, it will probably come off at the third _étape_ from here, when the party of prisoners is being taken to Siberia. Oh, that’s a long way off yet. Ivan Fyodorovitch has already visited the superintendent of the third _étape_. But we don’t know yet who will be in charge of the party, and it’s impossible to find that out so far ahead. Tomorrow perhaps I will show you the whole plan in detail. Ivan Fyodorovitch left it with me on the eve of the trial, in case it was needed.... That was when—do you remember?—you found us quarreling. He had just gone downstairs, but when I saw you I made him come back. Do you remember? Do you know what we were quarreling about then?”
“No, I don’t,” said Alyosha.

“Of course he didn’t tell you. It was about that plan of escape. He had told me the main idea three days before, and we started quarreling about it at once, and quarreled for three days. We quarreled because he told me that if Dmitri Fyodorovitch were convicted, he would escape abroad with that creature, and I felt furious at once—I can’t tell you why, I don’t even know myself why.... Oh, of course, I was furious about that creature, and that she, too, should go abroad with Dmitri!” Katerina Ivanovna exclaimed suddenly, her lips quivering with anger. “As soon as Ivan Fyodorovitch saw that I was furious about that woman, he instantly imagined I was jealous of Dmitri and that I still loved Dmitri. That is how our first quarrel began. I would not explain myself, and I could not ask forgiveness. I could not bear that such a man could suspect me of still loving that ... and when I myself had told him long before that I did not love Dmitri, that I loved no one but him! It was only my resentment against that creature that made me angry with him. Three days later, on the evening you came, he brought me a sealed envelope, which I was to open at once if anything happened to him. Oh, he foresaw his illness! He told me the envelope contained the details of the escape, and that if he died or fell dangerously ill, I was to save Mitya alone. Then he left me money, nearly ten thousand—those notes the prosecutor mentioned in his speech, having learned from someone that he had sent them to be changed. I was tremendously struck to find that Ivan Fyodorovitch had not given up his idea of saving his brother, and was trusting me with this plan of escape, though he was still jealous of me and still convinced that I loved Mitya. Oh, that was a sacrifice! No, you cannot understand the greatness of such self-sacrifice, Alexey Fyodorovitch. I wanted to fall at his feet in reverence, but I thought at once that he would take it only for joy at the thought of Mitya’s being saved (and he certainly would have imagined that!), and I was so exasperated at the mere possibility of such an unjust thought on his part that I lost my temper again, and instead of kissing his feet, I flew into a fury again! Oh, I am unhappy! It’s my character, my awful, unhappy character! Oh, you will see, I shall end by driving him, too, to leave me for another woman he can get on better with, like Dmitri. But ... no, I could not bear it, I would kill myself. And when you came in then, and I called to you and told him to come back, I was so enraged by the look of contempt and hatred he turned on me that—do you remember?—I cried out to you that it was he, he alone, who had persuaded me that his brother Dmitri was a murderer! I said that spiteful thing on purpose, to wound him again. He had never, never persuaded me that his brother was a murderer. On the contrary, it was I who persuaded him! Oh, my vile temper was the cause of everything! I paved the way to that hideous scene at the trial. He wanted to show me that he was an honorable man, and that even if I loved his brother, he would not ruin him out of revenge or jealousy. So he came to the court ... I am the cause of it all, I alone am to blame!”

Katya had never made such confessions to Alyosha before. He felt that she had now reached that stage of unbearable suffering when even the proudest heart painfully crushes its own pride and falls defeated by grief. Oh, Alyosha knew of another terrible reason for her misery, though she had carefully hidden it from him in the days since the trial. But for some reason it would have been too painful for him if she had been brought so low as to speak to him about that now. She was suffering for her “treachery” at the trial, and Alyosha felt that her conscience was driving her to confess it to him, to him, Alyosha, with tears and cries and hysterical writhing on the floor. But he dreaded that moment and longed to spare her. It made the errand he had come on even harder. He spoke of Mitya again.

“It’s all right, it’s all right, don’t be anxious about him!” she began again, sharply and stubbornly. “All that is only for the moment. I know him, I know his heart only too well. You can be sure he will agree to escape. It’s not as though it would happen right away. He will have time to make up his mind to it. Ivan Fyodorovitch will be well by then and will manage it all himself, so that I shall have nothing to do with it. Don’t be anxious. He will agree to run away. He has agreed already: do you think he would give up that creature? And they won’t let her go to him, so he is bound to escape. It’s you he’s most afraid of. He is afraid you won’t approve of his escape on moral grounds. But you must generously _allow_ it, if your blessing is so necessary,” Katya added viciously. She paused and smiled.

“He talks about some hymn,” she went on, “some cross he has to bear, some duty. I remember Ivan Fyodorovitch told me a great deal about it, and if you knew how he talked!” Katya cried suddenly, with a feeling she could not hold back. “If you knew how he loved that wretched man at the moment he told me, and how he hated him, perhaps, at the same moment. And I listened to his story and his tears with sneering contempt. Brute! Yes, I am a brute. I am to blame for his fever. But that man in prison is incapable of suffering,” Katya concluded irritably. “Can such a man suffer? Men like him never suffer!”

There was a note of hatred and contemptuous disgust in her words. And yet it was she who had betrayed him. “Perhaps because she feels how she has wronged him, she hates him at moments,” Alyosha thought to himself. He hoped it was only “at moments.” In Katya’s last words he heard a note of challenge, but he did not take it up.

“I sent for you this morning to make you promise to persuade him yourself. Or do you, too, think that escaping would be dishonorable, cowardly, or something ... unchristian, perhaps?” Katya added, even more defiantly.

“Oh, no. I’ll tell him everything,” muttered Alyosha. “He asks you to come and see him today,” he blurted out suddenly, looking her steadily in the face. She started, and drew back a little from him on the sofa.
“Me? Can that be?” she faltered, turning pale.

“It can be and it ought to be!” Alyosha began emphatically, growing more animated. “He needs you particularly just now. I wouldn’t have raised the subject and troubled you if it weren’t necessary. He is ill, he is beside himself, he keeps asking for you. He doesn’t want you in order to be reconciled with you, but only so that you will go and show yourself at his door. So much has happened to him since that day. He realizes that he has wronged you beyond all measure. He does not ask your forgiveness—‘It’s impossible to forgive me,’ he says himself—but only that you show yourself in his doorway.”
“It’s so sudden....” faltered Katya. “All these days I’ve had a feeling that you would come with this message. I knew he would ask me to come. It’s impossible!”

“Let it be impossible, but do it. Just think, he realizes for the first time how he has hurt you, the first time in his life. He had never understood it so fully before. He said, ‘If she refuses to come, I shall be unhappy all my life.’ Do you hear? Though he is sentenced to twenty years of penal servitude, he is still planning to be happy—isn’t that pitiful? Think—you must visit him. Though he is ruined, he is innocent,” broke from Alyosha like a challenge. “His hands are clean, there is no blood on them! For the sake of the infinite suffering ahead of him, visit him now. Go, greet him on his way into the darkness—stand at his door, that is all.... You ought to do it, you ought to!” Alyosha concluded, laying immense stress on the word “ought.”
“I ought to ... but I cannot....” Katya moaned. “He will look at me.... I can’t.”
“Your eyes ought to meet. How will you live the rest of your life, if you don’t make up your mind to it now?”
“Better to suffer all my life.”
“You ought to go, you ought to go,” Alyosha repeated with merciless emphasis.
“But why today, why at once?... I can’t leave our patient—”
“You can, for a moment. It will only be a moment. If you don’t come, he will be delirious by tonight. I wouldn’t tell you a lie. Have pity on him!”
“Have pity on _me!_” Katya said, with bitter reproach, and she burst into tears.
“Then you will come,” said Alyosha firmly, seeing her tears. “I’ll go and tell him you are coming right away.”
“No, don’t tell him that, not for anything,” cried Katya in alarm. “I will come, but don’t tell him beforehand, because perhaps I will go, but not go in.... I don’t know yet—”
Her voice failed her. She gasped for breath. Alyosha got up to go.
“And what if I meet anyone?” she said suddenly, in a low voice, turning white again.
“That’s exactly why you must go now, so you won’t meet anyone. There will be no one there, I can tell you that for certain. We will expect you,” he concluded emphatically, and went out of the room.
